label: Asthma flare-up
note:
The patient, a male, presented with shortness of breath and cough for two to three days, accompanied by fever and inability to complete sentences. He has a history of childhood asthma requiring hospitalisation and current hay fever, with no medication allergies. Examination revealed no chest pain, haemoptysis, or night-time symptoms, though exercise is currently impossible.

The working diagnosis is an asthma flare-up, possibly triggered by pollen or viral infection. The plan is to increase inhaler usage to two to four puffs every four hours, prescribe a spacer and peak flow meter, and advise regular antihistamines. A review is arranged in one week, with instructions to return if symptoms worsen or fever persists.
patient:
Your appointment today
You came because you could not breathe well. You also had a cough for a few days. You had a high temperature and could not speak in full sentences. You have a history of asthma from when you were a child. You also have hay fever right now. You do not have any allergies to medicines. We checked your chest and found no pain. You did not cough up blood. You do not have symptoms at night. You cannot exercise at the moment.

Your diagnosis
The working diagnosis is an asthma flare-up. This means your airways are narrowed. This makes it hard to breathe. It may be caused by pollen or a virus.

Your treatment and next steps
You will use your inhaler more often. Take two to four puffs every four hours. We will give you a spacer. This is a tube that helps the medicine go deeper. We will also give you a peak flow meter. This is a device to check your breathing speed. You should take antihistamines regularly. This medicine helps with hay fever symptoms. We will see you again in one week.

When to contact us
Return if your symptoms get worse. Return if your fever stays the same.

answers.happened: The history was hard to get: questions repeated, answers that contradicted each other, and a patient who said he could not finish sentences yet felt well sitting still. The childhood admissions for asthma came out only on direct questioning, and they changed how seriously I took a two-day wheeze.
answers.learned: Difficulty completing sentences is a severity marker even when it is reported casually, and a history of admissions raises the stakes. A remote consultation without a peak flow reading is working half blind, so getting a meter into the house was the most useful thing I did.
answers.next: I would ask the severity questions first and in the simplest words, and confirm the temperature reading rather than accepting a fever and a normal number in the same breath. A written plan for when to call back matters more than usual when the conversation itself was this hard.
